items.actClause: AN ACT to require the department of transportation to determine which entrances to parkways in the county of Westchester are most frequently accessed by oversized commercial vehicles and to install certain barriers to prevent such vehicles from accessing such entrances
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S5774

TITLE OF BILL:  An act to require the department of transportation to
determine which entrances to parkways in the county of Westchester are
most frequently accessed by oversized commercial vehicles and to
install certain barriers to prevent such vehicles from accessing such
entrances

PURPOSE:

To prevent oversized commercial vehicles from entering Westchester
County parkways.

SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 authorizes and directs the department of transportation to
determine which entrances to parkways in Westchester County are used
most frequently by oversized commercial vehicles and to install
barriers to prevent them from entering the parkway.

Section 2 authorizes the commissioner of the department of
transportation to obtain relevant information from state and local
agencies to help determine which entrances to Westchester County
parkways are most frequently accessed by oversized commercial
vehicles.

Section 3 is the effective date.

JUSTIFICATION:

Westchester County police statistics show that commercial trucks
wandered onto Westchester passenger-vehicle only parkways some 700-850
times a year for the last several years.

The dangers and damages caused by trucks entering parkways have
plagued Westchester County and the State for many years. Even where
this is no physical damage, a truck's travel on parkways creates
traffic chaos and a safety hazard to other motorists on a road
designed for passenger vehicles.

The Village of Rye Brook police statistics show that during a one-year
period there were 13 reports of commercial vehicles either hitting the
King Street overpass or traveling on the Hutchinson River Parkway.

While the Department of Transportation has taken some measures to
reduce the incidence of commercial vehicles on parkways the problem
still remains. The installation of truck barriers proposed by this
legislation would reduce accidents and hazards to motorists by
preventing oversized commercial vehicles from entering Westchester
County parkways at the entrances most frequently accessed by these
vehicles.

LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:


The cost will depend on the type and number of physical barriers
determined to be needed by the commissioner of the department of
transportation.

EFFECTIVE DATE:

The act shall take effect ninety days after it becomes law.

 TITLE OF BILL :  An act to require the department of transportation
to determine which entrances to parkways in the county of Westchester
are most frequently accessed by oversized commercial vehicles and to
install certain barriers to prevent such vehicles from accessing such
entrances

 PURPOSE :

To prevent oversized commercial vehicles from entering Westchester
County parkways.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section one authorizes and directs the department of transportation,
within one hundred twenty days, to study and determine which entrances
to special parkways in Westchester County are used most frequently by
commercial motor vehicles and, within one year of making such
determination, to install physical barriers to prevent or otherwise
hinder such commercial vehicles from accessing such parkways.

Section two authorizes the commissioner of the department of
transportation to request and receive, from any department, division,
board, bureau, commission or other agency of the state or any state
public authority such information and data as will enable the
department of transportation to properly conduct its study and make
its determinations.

Section three defines commercial motor vehicle and special parkways
for purposes of this act.

Section four is the effective date.

items.memoText:
VETO MESSAGE - No. 225

TO THE SENATE:

I am returning herewith, without my approval, the following bill:

Senate Bill Number 5774-A, entitled:

    "AN  ACT  to  require  the department of transportation to determine
      which entrances to parkways in the county of Westchester are  most
      frequently  accessed  by  oversized  commercial  vehicles  and  to
      install certain barriers to prevent such vehicles  from  accessing
      such entrances"

    NOT APPROVED

  This  bill  would  require  the  Department of Transportation (DOT) to
assess all entrances to Special Parkways in Westchester  County,  deter-
mine  which  entrances are most often used by oversized commercial vehi-
cles, and install physical barriers to prevent  entrance  of  commercial
vehicles at those access points.

  Although  I support the spirit of the legislation, it is fundamentally
flawed in several respects: (1) it presents a risk to public safety; (2)
the scheduled assessment has already been completed; and (3)  there  are
no funds appropriated to implement this duplicative assessment.

  Specifically, this bill would require DOT to install physical barriers
at  Parkway  access  points  to deter oversized commercial vehicles. But
such installation would pose a significant threat to  motorists.  It  is
well-established  that  the  required  barriers regularly sustain damage
when struck by vehicles, and may break apart and fall into  other  lanes
of  traffic.  Further, this bill would require DOT to conduct a study to
determine which entrances are most often used by  commercial  trucks  to
enter  Parkways  in Westchester County. But DOT has already completed an
assessment and is already focusing its resources on those entrances. DOT
has increased the visibility of  road  markings  and  signage  directing
these  vehicles  away  from parkway entrances. It has installed flashing
beacons and electronic variable message signs alerting truck drivers  of
travel  and bridge height restrictions. It has also enhanced the mapping
information available to truckers through GPS services, industry groups,
brochures, and the 511NY travel information service so they can  develop
alternate routes. DOT is also piloting a new active warning system which
uses  infrared  technology  to  detect  over-height  vehicles at Parkway
entrances. Finally, even if the agency were  to  conduct  a  duplicative
assessment, there is no appropriation for such an assessment which would
result in reductions elsewhere in DOT's capital plan.

  For these reasons, I am compelled to veto this bill.

  The bill is disapproved.                    (signed) ANDREW M. CUOMO
